title: The Ninth Legion: What the Evidence Says
requested_title: 5,000 Roman Soldiers Marched Into Britain & Never Came Back
visual_lock: Vertical 9:16 photoreal documentary reconstruction; Roman York and northern Britain, with map references to Nijmegen; naturalistic 35mm perspective; soft dawn or museum raking light; stone gray, parchment ochre, muted bronze and subdued iron red. No supernatural imagery or invented archival objects.
reference_sheet_prompt: Nano Banana Pro reference sheet, photoreal 9:16 documentary style: (1) stone gateway and fortress of Eboracum (Roman York), (2) close-up of authentic-looking Roman tile stamps and a weathered inscribed stone (reconstruction, not a claimed artifact photograph), (3) clean map locating York and Nijmegen. Natural 35mm lens perspective, soft dawn and museum raking light, Roman stone gray, parchment ochre, muted bronze, subdued iron red. No readable fabricated inscriptions, no battle outcome, no modern landmarks.
important_factual_note: Evidence note, checked 2026-10-26: RIB 665 dates the York building inscription to AD 107–108 and says the gate was built through Legion IX Hispana. RIB's tile-stamp catalogue places the Ninth's base at York from AD 71 until its probable departure toward the end of Trajan's reign, while noting stamped tiles at multiple sites. A 2025 Britannia/Cambridge article discusses possible Ninth detachments at Nijmegen in the early second century and last attested officers around AD 124; its broader Hadrianic-crisis connection is an interpretation, not proof of a specific defeat. The exact fate, battle, final headcount, and a 5,000-soldier disappearance are not established by these sources. Do not state that the entire legion was annihilated in Scotland.

blocks.source_notes: Evidence note, checked 2026-10-26: RIB 665 dates the York building inscription to AD 107–108 and says the gate was built through Legion IX Hispana. RIB's tile-stamp catalogue places the Ninth's base at York from AD 71 until its probable departure toward the end of Trajan's reign, while noting stamped tiles at multiple sites. A 2025 Britannia/Cambridge article discusses possible Ninth detachments at Nijmegen in the early second century and last attested officers around AD 124; its broader Hadrianic-crisis connection is an interpretation, not proof of a specific defeat. The exact fate, battle, final headcount, and a 5,000-soldier disappearance are not established by these sources. Do not state that the entire legion was annihilated in Scotland.
